elements.context: σωφροσύνης ἆρα οὐ δεήσει ἡμῖν τοῖς νεανίαις
σωφροσύνης δὲ ὡς πλήθει οὐ τὰ τοιάδε μέγιστα
εἴς γε σωφροσύνην νέοις ἐπιτήδεια ἀκούειν
Πηλέως, σωφρονεστάτου τε καὶ τρίτου ἀπὸ Διός

signals.observation: σωφροσύνη appears three times as a noun framing the discussion, then returns as the superlative adjective σωφρονεστάτου applied to Peleus in the characterization of Achilles' lineage.

elements.context: αὐτοὺς δὲ ἄρχοντας τῶν περὶ πότους καὶ ἀφροδίσια καὶ περὶ ἐδωδὰς ἡδονῶν

signals.observation: ἄρχων appears first as those to whom one is obedient, then as self-rule over pleasures, then as the target of insolent speech from private citizens—three distinct relations of ruling within a few lines.

elements.context: τῶν περὶ πότους καὶ ἀφροδίσια καὶ περὶ ἐδωδὰς ἡδονῶν
παρὰ πλεῖαι ὦσι τράπεζαι σίτου καὶ κρειῶν

signals.observation: The three pleasures named abstractly (drinking, sex, eating) at 389e are concretely instantiated in the Homeric quotations at 390b: full tables of food and meat, wine from the mixing-bowl, and death by hunger as its inversion.

elements.context: Ἄρεώς τε καὶ ἀφροδίτης ὑπὸ Ἡφαίστου δεσμόν

signals.observation: ἀφροδίσια first names a category of pleasure to be mastered, then appears as Zeus's overwhelming desire, then the proper name Ἀφροδίτη appears in the binding by Hephaestus—the abstract appetite becomes divine narrative.

elements.context: δῶρα θεοὺς πείθει, δῶρʼ αἰδοίους βασιλῆας
δῶρα μὲν λαβόντι ἐπαμύνειν τοῖς Ἀχαιοῖς
ἄνευ δὲ δώρων μὴ ἀπαλλάττεσθαι τῆς μήνιος

signals.observation: δῶρον appears five times in rapid succession: gifts persuade gods, gifts persuade kings, Phoenix advises accepting gifts, Achilles takes gifts from Agamemnon, and ransom for a corpse—all clustered around the prohibition on φιλοχρηματία.

elements.context: οὐ μὲν δὴ δωροδόκους γε ἐατέον εἶναι τοὺς ἄνδρας

signals.observation: φιλοχρήματος appears as a general prohibition, is then applied to Achilles, and intensifies into the noun φιλοχρηματία paired with ἀνελευθερία as one of two diseases in Achilles.

πείθω recurs densely across the section: gifts persuade gods; listeners must not be persuaded; we must not allow persuasion of our young; and one who is persuaded grants himself forgiveness—persuasion is both the danger and the mechanism being regulated.

elements.context: σιωπῇ ἧσο, ἐμῷ δʼ ἐπιπείθεο μύθῳ

signals.observation: Two Homeric quotations are placed in direct contrast: obedient silence addressed to a superior versus abusive address (dog-eyed, deer-hearted) from a private man to a ruler.
ἐγκράτεια (self-mastery) and καρτερία (endurance) name the positive capacity, while ἐπιθυμία names what overcomes Zeus—the section explicitly contrasts mastery and desire.

elements.form: στῆθος δὲ πλήξας κραδίην ἠνίπαπε μύθῳ

signals.observation: The approved Homeric example is a man striking his own chest and addressing his own heart with a command to endure—self-directed speech and self-directed physical action, unique among the quotations in the section.

Achilles is described as containing two diseases opposite to each other: servility-with-money-love and arrogance toward gods and men. The dual form νοσήματε δύο ἐναντίω ἀλλήλοιν is a striking formulation.

elements.context: περὶ γὰρ θεῶν ὡς δεῖ λέγεσθαι εἴρηται
οὐκοῦν καὶ περὶ ἀνθρώπων τὸ λοιπὸν εἴη ἄν

signals.observation: A fourfold descending sequence is enumerated: gods, daimons-and-heroes, those in Hades, humans—the first three are declared complete, the last is declared impossible to settle at present.

elements.context: ἀδύνατον δή, ὦ φίλε, ἡμῖν τοῦτό γε ἐν τῷ παρόντι τάξαι
ἡ δὲ δικαιοσύνη ἀλλότριον μὲν ἀγαθόν, οἰκεία δὲ ζημία

signals.observation: The section's final movement declares it impossible now (ἀδύνατον ἐν τῷ παρόντι) to legislate about humans until justice is discovered—the content-rules are explicitly suspended pending the finding of what justice is.
The poets' claim is stated as a chiastic contrast: unjust but happy, just but wretched—this is what the current discussion cannot yet refute.

elements.context: μηδέ τινʼ ἄλλον θεοῦ παῖδά τε καὶ ἥρω
Ἀχιλλεύς, θεᾶς ὢν παῖς καὶ Πηλέως

signals.observation: Divine parentage recurs insistently: child of a goddess, child of a god, near-sown of gods, children of gods, gods beget evils—the logic forces a disjunction: either the deeds are not theirs or they are not gods' children.
